name: Air New Zealand Limited
overview: Air New Zealand is the flag-carrier airline of New Zealand, operating an extensive domestic network (20+ destinations, ~380 flights/day) alongside international passenger and cargo services across the Pacific Rim - Australia, the Pacific Islands, Asia and North America - supported by bilateral alliance partners including United Airlines, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific and Air China. The airline is roughly 51% owned by the New Zealand Government (via the Crown), making it a quasi-strategic national asset as well as a listed equity. Revenue is generated primarily from passenger ticket sales (~87-90% of revenue), supplemented by cargo and a growing Airpoints loyalty/ancillary business.

business_model.summary: Air New Zealand earns revenue by selling passenger seats across domestic, Tasman/Pacific short-haul and long-haul international routes, plus air cargo capacity and ancillary/loyalty income. It is a capital-intensive, operationally-leveraged business: revenue is transactional (ticket-by-ticket) rather than recurring, though the Airpoints loyalty programme (5m+ members) and ancillary fees provide a smaller, stickier revenue stream. Profitability is highly sensitive to fuel prices, FX, capacity/fleet availability and macro-driven travel demand - as demonstrated starkly in FY2026 where a jet fuel price shock flipped a modestly profitable outlook into a NZ$340-390m pre-tax loss forecast.

revenue_streams.name: Passenger revenue (domestic + international)
revenue_streams.trend: mixed - H1 FY2026 passenger revenue +4% to $3.0bn on Tasman/Pacific capacity growth and premium mix, but domestic below expectations on soft business-purpose demand; includes $11m of Covid-era travel credit breakage

revenue_streams.name: Cargo
revenue_streams.trend: declining - H1 FY2026 cargo revenue down ~7% (down $23m ex-FX) on lower long-haul capacity/yields and rising Asia competition

revenue_streams.name: Contract services, other revenue and income (incl. engine compensation)
revenue_streams.trend: volatile - swings materially with one-off engine manufacturer compensation receipts (down to $55m in H1 FY2026 from $129m for all of FY2025, timing-dependent)

business_model.customer_type: B2C leisure and corporate/government travellers domestically and internationally; B2B cargo and contract/ground-handling services; loyalty ecosystem partners (retail, finance) via Airpoints
business_model.geographic_mix: Domestic New Zealand (~82-85% market share) is the core profit engine; international short-haul (Australia/Pacific) and long-haul (Asia, North America) provide network breadth and connect to global alliance partners; revenue and costs are heavily exposed to NZD/USD and NZD/AUD FX, with a weaker NZD in FY2026 adding to both revenue (favourable) and cost (unfavourable, e.g. USD fuel) volatility

competitive_position.market_position: Dominant domestic New Zealand carrier (historically ~82-85% market share), but this position is under sustained attack: Jetstar announced its largest-ever New Zealand/Tasman network expansion (2025/26), adding 660,000+ new seats, new domestic routes (e.g., Hamilton-Christchurch), with Jetstar fares typically running 40-50% below Air NZ on comparable routes. Internationally, Air NZ is a mid-sized network carrier reliant on bilateral partnerships (with United, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Air China) rather than full global alliance membership, competing against much larger full-service and low-cost carriers on long-haul legs.

moat_factors.description: Historically ~82-85% domestic market share and the most comprehensive NZ regional network provide a structural cost and reach advantage that is difficult for new entrants to replicate given NZ's small, geographically dispersed population - though this is now being tested by Jetstar's expansion

~51% Crown ownership provides implicit support (e.g., COVID-era recapitalisation) and slot/route access, but also invites political scrutiny of pricing, service levels and capital decisions, and can constrain purely commercial responses (e.g., fare-setting, cost cuts) during a downturn
Repeatedly named among the World's Safest Airlines; strong domestic brand loyalty and Airpoints programme (5m+ members, near-ubiquitous household penetration) support pricing and retention

Baa1 (Moody's) rating, one of the highest-rated airlines globally, gives access to capital at competitive rates versus most global peers; however net debt/EBITDA rose to 2.6x at 31 December 2025, above the 1.5x-2.5x target range, and is expected to remain elevated given the FY2026 loss

Bilateral partnerships with United, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific and Air China extend reach without full global-alliance capital commitment, though this is weaker than full alliance membership (e.g. Star Alliance, oneworld)

weaknesses: Small scale relative to global network carriers limits negotiating leverage with aircraft/engine OEMs, fuel suppliers and lessors
Reliance on a narrow set of long-haul routes and partner airlines for connectivity beyond the Pacific Rim
High fixed-cost base (aircraft ownership/leases, crew, engineering) with limited ability to flex quickly when demand or fuel costs move sharply
Domestic monopoly position now being directly challenged by Jetstar's aggressive capacity expansion and discount pricing

Heavy dependence on two engine manufacturers (Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce) whose global maintenance backlogs have grounded up to eight to eleven aircraft (~15-20% of the jet fleet) across FY2025 and H1 FY2026, a risk largely outside management's control
Government majority ownership can constrain some capital allocation/strategic flexibility (e.g., political sensitivity around fare increases, job cuts)
Net debt/EBITDA breached the top of its target range in H1 FY2026, reducing balance-sheet headroom just as a fuel-cost shock hit earnings

growth_drivers: Fleet renewal: first two of ten new GE-powered Boeing 787 aircraft due for delivery in H2 FY2026, supporting widebody capacity growth of ~20-25% over the following two years as engine constraints ease
Cabin/interior upgrades - including a newly announced refresh of the existing Boeing 777-300ER fleet interiors - lifting premium yields and customer experience alongside Dreamliner retrofits
Domestic and Tasman/Pacific network growth (e.g. two new A321neo aircraft added Tasman/Pacific Islands capacity in H1 FY2026)
Airpoints loyalty programme expansion - new partners driving ancillary/non-airline revenue and member engagement (5m+ members)
Kia Mau transformation/cost programme - ~$45m of incremental benefits in H1 FY2026 alone, ~$145m cumulative since inception, with up to a further ~NZ$100m of annualised cost savings targeted

New CEO-led company-wide strategy review (launched late 2025) aimed at resetting the operating model and returning the airline to sustained profitability through operational performance, growth and further cost transformation
Recovery of grounded fleet capacity through 2026-2027 as Pratt & Whitney/Rolls-Royce maintenance backlogs clear, unlocking pent-up capacity and productivity gains
Christchurch Engine Centre and other engineering infrastructure investment supporting long-term maintenance capability, resilience and a growing share-of-associate-earnings contribution

business.description: Up to eight to eleven aircraft (~15-20% of the jet fleet) grounded at times across FY2025/H1 FY2026 due to global Pratt & Whitney GTF and Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 maintenance backlogs; management expects only gradual improvement through H2 FY2026 and full resolution not until around calendar 2027, with financial benefit lagging any operational improvement because widebody capacity cannot be reintroduced and sold at short notice
Jetstar's largest-ever NZ network expansion (660,000+ new seats, new routes, fares 40-50% below Air NZ) directly threatens the domestic market share that anchors group profitability

Corporate/business-purpose travel demand has weakened materially and recovered slower than expected, compounding capacity constraints and pressuring yields; recent data shows Tasman/Pacific capacity up ~7.6% YoY while passenger numbers grew just 0.3%, evidencing soft underlying demand relative to capacity added

Long-serving CEO Greg Foran departed October 2025; successor Nikhil Ravishankar (former Chief Digital Officer) is new to the CEO role and has launched a company-wide strategy review, creating near-term execution and strategic uncertainty alongside broader executive team turnover (new COO, CCO, Chief Customer & Digital Officer all appointed since late 2025)
Cargo revenue fell ~7% in H1 FY2026 on reduced long-haul capacity, lower load factors and increased Asia-market competition

financial.description: Middle East conflict escalation (Q1 2026) drove jet fuel from ~US$85-90/bbl to a peak of ~US$150-230/bbl; H2 FY2026 fuel costs are now expected at ~NZ$980m versus NZ$740m assumed at the February 2026 interim result, a ~NZ$240m headwind that hedging only partially offsets (every US$10/bbl move shifts the annual fuel bill by ~NZ$55m)
Revenue and costs (fuel, aircraft leases/debt, engineering) are USD/AUD-exposed; a weaker NZD in H1 FY2026 added to non-fuel cost inflation and fuel costs even as underlying USD jet fuel prices fell

Net debt/EBITDA rose to 2.6x at 31 December 2025, above the 1.5x-2.5x Capital Management Framework target range, and management expects it to remain elevated in the short term as earnings fall and fleet/interior capex continues

Engine manufacturer compensation (NZ$129m FY2025, NZ$55m H1 FY2026, down from prior-period levels) partially offsets grounding costs, but H2 FY2026 compensation arrangements were not yet agreed as of the interim result and timing/quantum remain uncertain and could materially affect full-year earnings

No interim dividend was declared for H1 FY2026, consistent with the Capital Management Framework, as the Board prioritises balance-sheet resilience over distributions while conditions remain challenging

regulatory.description: ~51% Crown shareholding creates potential for political/strategic considerations (regional route obligations, fare scrutiny, ESG mandates) to override pure commercial decision-making

regulatory.risk: Rising aviation sector levies and charges
regulatory.description: Mandated passenger levies, engineering/maintenance-related charges and domestic airport landing charges have risen materially ahead of NZ CPI and are a key driver (~$75m in H1 FY2026) of non-fuel cost inflation; management has flagged concern about the future trajectory of these industry-wide costs and their impact on affordability and regional connectivity

CORSIA carbon-offset obligations are already a rising cost input; longer-term 2030 emissions-reduction and SAF targets require sustained investment, and SAF availability/cost and future carbon-pricing changes remain constraints

macro.description: Geopolitical shocks (Middle East conflict, Strait of Hormuz disruption risk) demonstrated how quickly fuel costs can swing FY earnings from a modest profit outlook to a large loss; fuel is Air NZ's largest and least controllable cost
Domestic corporate/government travel and consumer discretionary leisure spend are cyclical and have softened amid a weak NZ economy
Engine and aircraft parts shortages are an industry-wide phenomenon (affecting many GTF/Trent operators globally), meaning resolution timing is largely outside Air NZ's control

Aircraft financing/leasing costs are sensitive to global interest rates; the investment-grade rating helps mitigate but does not eliminate this exposure, and is itself now under some pressure from elevated leverage

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global and Asia-Pacific aviation demand has broadly normalised post-COVID, but 2025-2026 has been marked by an industry-wide engine durability crisis (GTF, Trent 1000) grounding aircraft globally, and a sharp, geopolitically-driven jet fuel cost shock in H1 calendar 2026. NZ domestic aviation is entering a more competitive, lower-fare era as Jetstar scales up, while aviation-system levies/charges are rising structurally ahead of CPI.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - airlines are classic capital-intensive cyclicals; earnings swing sharply with fuel prices, FX, and consumer/corporate travel demand, as evidenced by the swing from $222m EBT (FY2024) to $189m (FY2025) to a $144m H1 FY2025 profit followed by a $59m H1 FY2026 loss and an expected $340-390m full-year FY2026 pre-tax loss
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - significant fleet financing/lease obligations mean higher rates raise the cost of capital for aircraft acquisition, though the Baa1 investment-grade rating (now under some pressure from elevated leverage) provides relatively favourable access to debt markets
key_input_costs: Jet fuel (largest single cost, highly volatile - spiked to ~US$150-230/bbl from ~US$85-90/bbl in H1 calendar 2026)
Labour (pilots, cabin crew, engineers) - +3.2% in H1 FY2026
Aviation sector levies and airport charges - rising materially ahead of NZ CPI
Foreign exchange (USD-denominated fuel/lease costs vs NZD revenue; weaker NZD added cost pressure in H1 FY2026)

recent_developments.event: FY2025 result: EBT of $189m (down from $222m), NPAT $126m (down 14%); engine availability constraints estimated to have cost ~$165m of EBT; up to 11 aircraft (~20% of jet fleet) grounded at times; $129m compensation received from engine manufacturers
CEO Greg Foran announced departure after ~6 years leading the airline through COVID and recovery; Nikhil Ravishankar (Chief Digital Officer) named successor, effective 20 October 2025
Final FY2025 unimputed dividend of 1.25 cps paid; total FY2025 dividends 2.5 cps; share buyback (announced Feb 2025) continued, with $81m repurchased cumulatively by 31 Dec 2025
Jetstar announced its largest-ever NZ/Tasman network expansion - 660,000+ new annual seats, new domestic routes (e.g. Hamilton-Christchurch from 1 Dec 2025), intensifying domestic competition

New CEO Nikhil Ravishankar launched a company-wide strategy review; executive team refreshed with new Chief Operations Officer (Kate Boyer), Chief Customer and Digital Officer (Jeremy O'Brien) and Chief Commercial Officer (Scott Wilkinson, also overseeing Loyalty); COO Alex Marren retired end of March 2026

H1 FY2026 (six months to 31 Dec 2025) result: pre-tax loss of $59m and net loss after tax of $40m (vs $144m EBT/$98m NPAT pcp); passenger revenue +4% to $3.0bn, operating costs including fuel +8%; net debt/EBITDA rose to 2.6x, above the 1.5x-2.5x target range; $55m engine compensation received but ~$90m of estimated lost earnings from continued groundings (up to eight aircraft grounded at times); no interim dividend declared, consistent with the Capital Management Framework; initial FY2026 guidance was for H2 earnings broadly in line with/modestly below H1, assuming US$85/bbl jet fuel

Air New Zealand suspended FY2026 earnings guidance, citing 'unprecedented volatility' in jet fuel markets following Middle East conflict escalation and closure risk to the Strait of Hormuz; jet fuel spiked from ~US$85-90/bbl to ~US$150-230/bbl over a matter of weeks

Air New Zealand issued updated FY2026 outlook: full-year pre-tax LOSS of NZ$340-390m, versus prior expectations of second-half earnings broadly in line with/modestly below the H1 loss; H2 fuel costs now forecast at ~NZ$980m vs NZ$740m assumed in February; announced ~NZ$70m of mitigating fare increases and network-wide capacity reductions of 3-5%, plus identification of up to NZ$100m of annualised cost savings

Management reported improving trajectory on Boeing 787 fleet availability heading into H2 FY2026, with full Airbus neo fleet targeted for calendar 2027; first two of ten new GE-powered Boeing 787s due for delivery later in FY2026, supporting a targeted ~20-25% widebody capacity increase over the following two years

Trading update noted Tasman/Pacific capacity up ~7.6% YoY versus passenger growth of just 0.3%, evidencing soft demand relative to added capacity; also confirmed reduced flying on several routes due to elevated jet fuel prices; commentary framed the situation as expected to improve over time as fuel/fleet pressures ease

Air New Zealand confirmed FY2026 annual results (year ended 30 June 2026) will be released before market open on 28 August 2026, with a live investor/analyst conference call hosted by CEO Nikhil Ravishankar and CFO Richard Thomson; shares have traded in a roughly NZ$0.42-0.56 range through July-August 2026 (analyst consensus target ~NZ$0.41, below spot), with Jarden downgrading to Sell (target NZ$0.47) in March 2026 amid the fuel-driven guidance cut; consensus FY2026 EPS estimates have fallen sharply (to roughly NZ$0.03) even as revenue forecasts have been nudged up

guidance.as_of: May 2026 trading update (post H1 FY2026 result); FY2026 annual result due 28 August 2026

items.notes: Reversed from a small full-year profit expectation at the Feb 2026 interim result; driven by a ~NZ$240m H2 fuel cost headwind (fuel now expected at ~NZ$980m in H2 vs NZ$740m assumed at Feb interim) following the 2026 Middle East-driven jet fuel price shock; compensation arrangements for H2 not yet agreed, adding further uncertainty

items.vs_prior: lowered - new mitigating action announced May 2026
items.notes: Announced alongside ~NZ$70m of fare increases as mitigating actions against the fuel cost shock; August 2026 trading commentary confirmed reduced flying on several routes due to elevated jet fuel prices

items.target: Up to NZ$100 million annualised (incremental to Kia Mau's existing ~$145m cumulative benefits)
items.notes: Accelerated cost-reduction initiatives begun in late 2025 under new CEO, plus a review of capital expenditure plans as part of the broader strategy reset

items.target: ~20-25% growth over the next two years
items.notes: Driven by delivery of ten new GE-powered Boeing 787s (first two due H2 FY2026) as engine-related groundings gradually ease

items.notes: Engine maintenance-related groundings expected to ease materially through 2026 and largely resolve by end of calendar 2027; management cautions the financial benefit lags operational improvement since widebody capacity cannot be reintroduced and sold at short notice

Board prioritising balance-sheet resilience and financial flexibility given uncertainty across fleet availability, compensation and fuel costs; final FY2026 dividend also at risk given the guided full-year loss

guidance.management_commentary: New CEO Nikhil Ravishankar (effective Oct 2025, first results as CEO in Feb 2026) has launched a company-wide strategy review targeting a reset of the operating model, citing a fundamentally different cost environment (structural aviation-system inflation, not just cyclical pressure). His stated near-term priorities: safe/punctual/world-class service, profit improvement and cost-base review, working with engine manufacturers to accelerate aircraft returns, advocacy for a fairer aviation cost system, and the strategy review itself. Chair Dame Therese Walsh characterised the fuel price shock as a material external shock outside the company's control, distinct from the engine-availability issues that dominated FY2025/H1 FY2026, and reiterated the Board's commitment to the investment-grade credit rating and Capital Management Framework (liquidity target $1.2-1.5bn, net debt/EBITDA 1.5x-2.5x, dividend payout 40-70% of underlying NPAT) even as near-term distributions are curtailed. Management does not expect fleet availability improvements to translate immediately into earnings uplift given diseconomies of scale from disrupted operations, but expects improved resilience into FY2027. FY2026 annual results (due 28 August 2026) will be the next major checkpoint on whether the guided $340-390m pre-tax loss, cost-savings trajectory and fleet recovery timeline are tracking as flagged in May 2026.

bull_case: Domestic network density and historically ~82-85% market share remain a structural advantage even as Jetstar expands, given New Zealand's small, dispersed population and high barriers to entry

Engine availability crisis is a transient, industry-wide (not Air NZ-specific) problem showing early signs of improvement into H2 FY2026, with new GE-powered 787 deliveries and full neo-fleet resolution targeted by calendar 2027, unlocking pent-up capacity and productivity gains

Government majority ownership (~51%) and Baa1 investment-grade credit rating (even if under some pressure) provide a funding/support backstop unusual among global airlines, reducing solvency risk through severe downturns

New CEO-led strategy review and accelerated Kia Mau cost programme (up to NZ$100m of additional annualised savings targeted) could structurally reset the cost base and restore margins once fuel/engine headwinds normalise

Shares have recovered off their 2026 lows toward the NZ$0.42-0.56 range ahead of the 28 August FY2026 result, suggesting some of the fuel-shock bad news may already be discounted, with recovery optionality once fuel prices normalise, the fleet is fully available, and the annual result clarifies the earnings trough
bear_case: FY2026 pre-tax loss of NZ$340-390m marks a severe earnings reversal driven by a fuel cost shock that is inherently unpredictable and could recur or persist longer than currently modelled, with H2 compensation still unagreed as of the interim result

Jetstar's aggressive, structurally lower-cost expansion into NZ domestic and Tasman routes threatens to erode Air NZ's core profit engine (domestic market share) over the medium term, compounding a slower-than-expected domestic demand recovery (August 2026 data showed Tasman/Pacific capacity +7.6% YoY against passenger growth of only 0.3%)

Engine-related groundings have now persisted for multiple consecutive years (FY2025 and H1 FY2026), with management's own timelines for full resolution repeatedly extended, suggesting execution/visibility risk even as some early signs of improvement emerge

Net debt/EBITDA (2.6x) already above the top of the 1.5x-2.5x target range, dividends suspended, and rising structural aviation-system levies/charges add further balance-sheet and margin pressure just as the fuel shock hits

New CEO and largely refreshed executive team (COO, CCO, Chief Customer & Digital Officer all new since late 2025) mid-strategy-review creates execution and strategic-direction uncertainty at a critical juncture, with analyst consensus (e.g. Jarden's March 2026 Sell rating, ~NZ$0.41 average target) skewed negative relative to the current share price
